GLOBAL DETERMINATION FOR AN INVERSE PROBLEM FROM
THE VORTEX DYNAMICS
RU-YU LAI AND HANMING ZHOU
Abstract. We consider the problem of reconstructing a background potential from
the dynamical behavior of vortex dipole. We prove that under suitable conditions,
one can uniquely reconstruct a real-analytic potential by measuring the entrance and
exit positions as well as travel times between boundary points. In particular, the work
removes the ﬂatness assumption on the potential from the earlier result. A key step
of our method is a constructional procedure of recovering the boundary jet of the
potential.
1. Introduction
We study the reconstruction of a background potential from the dynamics of vortices.
We consider a pair of vortices {a+, a−} of opposite charge (vortex dipole) govern by the
following ODE system in R2:

The main objective of our work is to study the inverse problem for the reconstruction of
the background potential Q(x) from the travel information of the dipole. The uniqueness
result for this inverse problem was ﬁrst proved in [4] when the potential is suﬃciently
smooth and ﬂat, indicating the path of the dipole is close to straight lines. Speciﬁcally,
in [4], the potential is uniquely identiﬁed by using the trajectory of the center of mass of
the dipole. A reconstruction formula for the potential and numerical examples are also
investigated in [4].

The inverse problem under study is the determination of the potential Q in Ωfrom
measurements S. As mentioned above, the unique determination result of a background
potential from the trajectories of vortex dipole was studied in [4], under the assumption
that the potential is almost ﬂat in a suitable space. The measurements taken in [4] are
regarding the Hamiltonian ﬂow of the dipole center, i.e. (a++a−)/2, while in the current
paper, we measure the trajectories of a+ and a−separately without knowing the phase
(velocity vector) information. In other words, the inverse problem under consideration
only uses phaseless data, which is more applicable in practice.
The main strategy consists of two steps - local determination and global determination.
We ﬁrst show that all the derivatives of the potential Q at a boundary point on ∂Ω,
i.e. the boundary jet of Q, can be reconstructed from S, see Theorem 1.1. Then this
established local result yields the global reconstruction of Q in Theorem 1.2 due to the
analytic assumption of Q.
To achieve this goal, we need an assumption on the convexity of the boundary w.r.t.
the potential which is stated in the following deﬁnition.
Deﬁnition 1.1. Let p ∈∂Ω, we say that the boundary ∂Ωis strictly convex at p w.r.t.
the background potential Q if there exists a small open neighborhood Vp of p, such that
a+(s, p, q) /∈Ω, s ∈(−δ, δ) \ {0} for some δ > 0, whenever q ∈Vp \ Ω, q ̸= p, satisfying
˙a+(0, p, q) tangent to ∂Ω.
For example, given a bounded domain Ωwith strictly convex boundary (w.r.t. the
Euclidean metric) and p ∈∂Ω, we assume that |∇Q(p)| is suﬃciently small, then ∂Ωis
strictly convex at p w.r.t. Q (viewed as a small perturbation of trivial potential). Note
that even though we deﬁne the convexity by looking at the trajectory a+, Deﬁnition 1.1
could also be deﬁned in terms of a−due to the symmetry of a+ and a−in the ODEs
(1.1).

Theorem 1.1 immediately implies the global determination of real-analytic background
potentials. Notice that a convex domain is path-connected.
Theorem 1.2 (Global determination). Let Q ∈C∞(R2) be a background potential and
let Ω⊂R2 be a bounded convex open domain with smooth boundary. Suppose that ∂Ω
is strictly convex w.r.t. Q at some point on ∂Ω. There exists an open neighborhood eΩ
of Ω. Suppose, in addition, that Q is known in R2 \ eΩand real-analytic in eΩ. Then for
any open neighborhood U of eΩ, the measurement S in U \ Ωdetermines Q in eΩ.
1.2. Methodology. In this paper, we are motivated by the techniques developed in
the study of classical geometric inverse problem, namely the boundary rigidity problem,
which consists of determining a Riemannian metric on a compact smooth manifold with
boundary from the collection of distance (w.r.t. the metric) between pairs of boundary
points. This problem arises naturally from the geophysical question of recovering the
inner structure of the Earth from the travel time of seismic waves. We refer interested

readers to the survey paper [13] and the references therein for recent developments of
the boundary rigidity and related problems.
A key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 1.1 is an integral identity ﬁrst derived by
Stefanov and Uhlmann [10] in the study of the boundary rigidity problem for almost ﬂat
metrics. The integral identity works for general ﬂows given by the solutions of governing
ODE system. In our case, it connects the diﬀerence of measurement operators of two
potentials Q1 and Q2 with some weighted integral of the diﬀerence of Hamiltonian vector
ﬁelds of Q1 and Q2, see (3.1). In particular, we let Q2 = 0, the trivial potential, and
repeatedly diﬀerentiate the integral to recover all the derivatives of Q1 at a boundary
point.
Notice that our approach of the boundary determination of the potential is
constructional. The integral identity has also been used in the study of the boundary and
global determination questions in various inverse problems, e.g. the boundary rigidity
problem [1, 11, 12, 18, 19, 20], the non-abelian Radon transform [8, 21] and the lens
rigidity problem for Yang-Mills potentials [9, 22].
The paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we discuss the construction of the
domain eΩand the preliminary setting for the problem under study. Section 3 is devoted
to recovering the derivatives of the potential at a given boundary point by applying the
Stefanov-Uhlmann identity. Then in Section 4, the global determination of the potential
follows by using the local result in Section 3 and the analyticity of the potential. Finally,
additional useful lemmas are placed in the Appendix A.

3. Determination of the boundary jet
In this section, we will show the local reconstruction of Q from the measurement S.
This section consists of two main parts. In Section 3.1, we ﬁrst introduce the Stefanov-
Uhlmann identity. This identity connects the data S to the discrepancy in the two vortex
dynamic in a given potential (we will take the given one to be trivial potential Q0) and
the unknown potential Q, respectively. Then we will apply this identity to recover such
potential Q in Section 3.2.

4. Global reconstruction of real-analytic potentials
Based on the local result in Section 3, we can now determine Q globally in eΩ.
Proof of Theorem 1.2. The hypothesis of the theorem gives that ∂Ωis strictly convex at
some point p ∈∂Ωw.r.t. the potential Q. By Theorem 1.1 (also Theorem 3.1), ∂αQ(p)
is recovered for any multi-index α, |α| ≥1 from the data S. Notice that eΩis an open
neighborhood of Ω, then it implies that p is actually an interior point of eΩ. Since Q is
real-analytic in eΩ, so is ∇Q. Thus, we can uniquely recover ∇Q in some neighborhood
of p. Moreover, since eΩis path-connected and ∇Q is analytic, we can then determine
∇Q uniquely in the whole domain eΩ.

GLOBAL DETERMINATION FOR AN INVERSE PROBLEM FROM VORTEX DYNAMICS

Abstract: We consider the problem of reconstructing a background potential from the dynamical behavior of vortex dipole. We prove that under suitable conditions, one can uniquely reconstruct a real-analytic potential by measuring the entrance and exit positions as well as travel times between boundary points. In particular, the work removes the ﬂatness assumption on the potential from the earlier result. A key step of our method is a constructional procedure of recovering the boundary jet of the potential.
